vignette:
He is 64, a South Asian man who has spent most of his adult life working with his hands. For years he has worked in a warehouse, the kind of job where the day is measured by pallets, forklifts, inventory sheets, and the familiar ache in his shoulders by evening. He is known there as dependable and quiet. He arrives early, drinks tea from a thermos, and keeps mostly to himself. The men he works with know him as steady. His wife knows how much effort that steadiness costs him.

Many years ago, before he came to this country, he was taken and held captive for several days during a period of political unrest in his home region. He does not tell the story all at once. It emerges over several sessions, in fragments, with long silences between them. He had been traveling home from work when armed men stopped the bus. He remembers being forced out with several other men, his face covered, his hands tied so tightly that he lost feeling in them. He was held in a small dark room with little air, unsure if it was day or night. He could hear footsteps in the corridor, metal scraping, distant shouting, and sometimes cries from other rooms. The uncertainty was its own form of torture. He never knew when someone would open the door, whether he would be beaten, questioned, or simply left alone with his fear. He remembers trying to keep track of time by reciting prayers and mentally naming family members, as if keeping their names in his mind might keep him alive.

He was eventually released without explanation. By then he had lost weight, his body bruised and weak, but what stays with him most is the feeling that the world had become unpredictable and unsafe. In the immediate aftermath, he tells himself he must act normal. His family is relieved he is home, and he tries to be grateful and silent. Instead, he becomes watchful. Ordinary noises make his body jolt. If someone comes up behind him, his chest tightens before he can think. At night he lies awake, listening for movement outside. When he does sleep, he wakes in panic, soaked in sweat, certain for a few seconds that he is back in that airless room. His wife reaches for him and he sometimes pulls away before realizing where he is.

After immigrating, he throws himself into work. The warehouse suits him in some ways. The tasks are concrete, repetitive, and physical. He likes knowing where things belong, likes the relief of order. But the environment also provokes him. When the loading dock doors slam, he startles visibly. If a forklift backfires or a metal crate drops, his whole body goes rigid. He scans the room automatically, locating exits before he begins a shift. He prefers working in open aisles where he can see who is approaching. If asked to check stock in a cramped storage cage or windowless container, he feels his throat close and finds a reason to switch tasks with someone else. He tells coworkers he has bad knees or needs more light, and they accept this, though a few have noticed that he avoids enclosed spaces with unusual determination.

At home, captivity continues to shape the rhythm of family life. His wife says he has become more distant over the years, not unkind but hard to reach. He sits with his back to the wall in restaurants. He checks the locks repeatedly before bed. He dislikes crowds, unexpected visitors, and any change in routine. His children, now grown, learned early not to jump on him or cover his eyes in play. He feels ashamed of how irritable he can become over small things: a door left ajar, a late arrival, the television turned up too loud. Sometimes he hears himself snapping and sees fear or confusion in his wife’s face, and then he goes quiet for the rest of the evening.

He does not often speak about what happened because speaking makes it vivid. Still, memories intrude without permission. The smell of damp cardboard in the warehouse after rain can suddenly bring back the room where he was held. Darkness during a power outage makes him feel trapped in his own house. Certain dialects, certain boots, even the rattle of keys can transport him instantly. In those moments he is no longer a man nearing retirement, sorting shipments under fluorescent lights. He is again a younger man counting breaths in the dark, waiting for a door to open.

What troubles him now is not only the fear but the endurance of it. He says he knows, logically, that he is safe, that those days are long behind him. But his body does not believe what his mind knows. He is tired from years of poor sleep, tired from carrying vigilance like a second job. He wants to enjoy ordinary things—morning tea with his wife, visits from his grandchildren, a quiet shift at work—but he moves through life as if danger might still step out from behind a closed door.
